chapters.1: This chapter gives instructions for the burnt offering, a sacrifice in which an animal from the herd, flock, or birds is completely burned on the altar as a pleasing act of worship to God. It details the specific steps worshippers and priests must follow depending on whether the offering is a bull, a sheep or goat, or a bird.
chapters.2: This chapter covers the grain (meat) offering, made of fine flour, oil, and frankincense, either raw or baked in various ways, with a portion burned on the altar and the rest given to the priests to eat. It specifies that these offerings must never contain leaven or honey but must always include salt.
chapters.3: This chapter describes the peace offering, a voluntary sacrifice of an animal from the herd or flock, male or female, where the fat portions are burned on the altar as food for God by fire. It restates the permanent rule that the Israelites must never eat fat or blood.
chapters.4: This chapter explains the sin offering required when someone unintentionally breaks one of God's commands, with different animals specified depending on whether the offender is the high priest, the whole community, a leader, or an ordinary person. In each case, the animal's blood and fat are handled in a prescribed way to make atonement so the sin is forgiven.
chapters.5: This chapter continues the sin and guilt (trespass) offerings, covering cases like failing to testify, touching something unclean, or making a careless oath, and allows cheaper offerings like birds or flour for those who cannot afford an animal. It also addresses guilt offerings for unintentional wrongs against holy things, requiring restitution plus the sacrifice.
chapters.6: This chapter gives further rules for restitution when someone sins by lying, stealing, or swearing falsely about property, requiring repayment plus a fifth extra along with a guilt offering. It then details the priests' duties for keeping the altar fire burning continually and for handling the burnt offering, the grain offering, and the sin offering.
chapters.7: This chapter finishes the instructions for the guilt (trespass) offering and the peace offering, including rules on how soon the meat must be eaten and specifying which portions, like the breast and right thigh, belong to the priests. It closes by summarizing the laws covering all five major types of sacrifice given to Moses at Mount Sinai.
chapters.8: Moses formally ordains Aaron and his sons as priests exactly as God commanded, washing them, dressing Aaron in his priestly garments, anointing him with oil, and offering a bull and two rams as sin, burnt, and ordination offerings. The ceremony concludes with Aaron and his sons required to stay at the tabernacle entrance for seven full days to complete their consecration.
chapters.9: On the eighth day, Aaron begins his priestly duties by offering sacrifices first for himself and then for the people, following Moses' instructions exactly. After the offerings are completed, Aaron blesses the people, and fire comes out from before the Lord and consumes the offering on the altar, causing the people to shout and fall facedown in awe.
chapters.10: Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu offer unauthorized "strange fire" before the Lord and are instantly struck dead by fire from God as a result. Moses instructs the rest of Aaron's family not to mourn outwardly so as not to profane their priestly duties, and gives further instructions about priests avoiding alcohol on duty and properly eating their portions of the offerings.
chapters.11: This chapter lists which animals are clean and may be eaten and which are unclean and forbidden, covering land animals (like approving ones that chew the cud and have split hooves, while excluding pigs and camels), water creatures with fins and scales, certain birds, and insects, allowing only certain locust-type insects. It also explains how contact with unclean animal carcasses makes a person or object ceremonially unclean.
chapters.12: This short chapter sets out purification rules for a woman after childbirth, specifying a longer period of ceremonial uncleanness and purification after a daughter than after a son, after which she must bring a lamb and a bird, or two birds if she cannot afford a lamb, as offerings to be made clean again.
chapters.13: This chapter gives detailed diagnostic criteria for priests to examine skin conditions, sores, and rashes to determine whether they are a contagious "leprosy" (a broader category of skin disease) making a person unclean, including signs like white hair or spreading sores, with periods of quarantine and reexamination. It also covers how to identify this kind of mildew-like contamination in clothing and fabric.
chapters.14: This chapter details the ritual for cleansing a person once their skin disease has healed, involving sacrifices, shaving, washing, and the release of a live bird, with a simpler version allowed for the poor. It also explains how priests are to diagnose and remedy a similar contamination found growing in the walls of a house, including tearing out affected stones or, if it persists, demolishing the house entirely.
chapters.15: This chapter addresses ceremonial uncleanness connected to bodily discharges, including issues affecting men, nocturnal emissions, and a woman's monthly menstrual period or prolonged bleeding, specifying washing and waiting periods to become clean again. It emphasizes keeping the camp and tabernacle free from this kind of uncleanness.
chapters.16: This chapter establishes the Day of Atonement, the one day each year when the high priest enters the Most Holy Place to make atonement for himself, his household, and the whole nation using the blood of a bull and a goat. A second goat, the "scapegoat," has the people's sins symbolically placed on it before being sent out into the wilderness, and the day is set as a permanent annual observance of rest and repentance.
chapters.17: This chapter requires that any animal slaughtered for food be brought to the tabernacle as an offering rather than killed informally, to prevent sacrifices to other gods, and strictly forbids eating blood because the blood represents the life God has set apart for atonement. It applies these rules equally to native Israelites and to foreigners living among them.
chapters.18: This chapter lists forbidden sexual relationships, mainly incest with various close relatives such as parents, siblings, aunts, uncles, in-laws, and sex during a woman's menstrual period, also forbidding child sacrifice to the god Molech and same-sex relations. These practices are described as defiling, associated with the nations God is removing from Canaan, and reasons the land itself can reject its inhabitants.
chapters.19: This wide-ranging chapter calls Israel to be holy as God is holy, covering honoring parents, keeping the Sabbath, avoiding idols, leaving gleanings in fields for the poor, honest business dealings, loving one's neighbor as oneself, and fair treatment of foreigners, the elderly, and the disabled. It also bans mixing certain things like crops, fabrics, and animal breeding, along with pagan mourning and divination practices.
chapters.20: This chapter sets out serious penalties, often death, for major violations including child sacrifice to Molech, consulting mediums or spiritists, cursing one's parents, adultery, and the incestuous and other sexual sins listed earlier in Leviticus 18. It frames these commands as what sets Israel apart as God's holy people distinct from the practices of the nations being displaced from Canaan.
chapters.21: This chapter gives special holiness requirements for priests, limiting their contact with dead bodies to close relatives, restricting who they may marry, and forbidding certain mourning customs because of their sacred role. It also states that priests with physical disabilities or blemishes, while still provided for, may not personally perform sacrifices at the altar.
chapters.22: This chapter sets rules ensuring priests only handle holy offerings while ceremonially clean, and restricts who outside a priest's household may eat the sacred food. It also specifies that animals offered as sacrifices must be healthy and without physical defects, reinforcing that only the best is acceptable to God.
chapters.23: This chapter lays out Israel's annual festival calendar: the weekly Sabbath, Passover and Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Firstfruits, Pentecost (the Feast of Weeks), the Feast of Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and the Feast of Tabernacles, during which people lived in temporary shelters. Each festival has its own specified offerings, days of rest from work, and dates within Israel's religious calendar.
chapters.24: This chapter gives instructions for keeping oil lamps burning continually in the tabernacle and setting out twelve loaves of bread each week as an offering for the priests. It then recounts an incident where a man blasphemes God's name during a quarrel and is stoned to death by the whole community, prompting a restatement of the principle of equal justice, including "eye for eye," for both Israelites and foreigners.
chapters.25: This chapter establishes the sabbatical year, when fields must lie fallow every seventh year, and the Year of Jubilee every fiftieth year, when land returns to its original family owners and Israelite slaves are freed. It sets rules for fair pricing of land and property based on years remaining until Jubilee and requires compassionate treatment of the poor and of Israelites who become servants due to debt.
chapters.26: This chapter presents God's covenant blessings for obedience, including abundant harvests, peace, and safety, contrasted with escalating curses for disobedience, including disease, famine, defeat by enemies, and eventual exile from the land. It ends on a note of hope, promising that even in exile, if the people humble themselves and confess, God will remember his covenant with their ancestors and not abandon them completely.
chapters.27: This closing chapter covers the valuation and redemption of vows made to God, including vows involving people, animals, houses, and fields, with fixed monetary values set by age and sex and extra payment required to redeem rather than fulfill a vowed item. It concludes by affirming that tithes of crops and livestock belong to the Lord as holy.
